account: On 23 June 2021 the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam displayed Rembrandt's The Night Watch with reconstructions of the strips cut from all four sides in 1715. The canvas had been trimmed to fit a wall in the Town Hall. Rijksmuseum senior scientist Robert Erdmann trained artificial neural networks on the original and on a seventeenth-century copy attributed to Gerrit Lundens. The networks generated the missing sections in Rembrandt's style. Printed reconstructions were mounted around the original for the following months. The remaining original canvas measures 379.5 by 436 centimeters. The museum gives the result as a reconstruction of 393.1 by 507.4 centimeters, with strips of 64.4 cm on the left, 7 cm on the right, 23.3 cm at the top and 11.3 cm at the bottom. Director Taco Dibbits said: “Thanks to this reconstruction, we can now see that the composition as it was painted by Rembrandt was even more dynamic.” Hyperallergic reported the project independently on 24 June 2021. On 18 August 2026, two scholars at the Repin Academy of Fine Arts in St Petersburg, who have no tie to the museum, published an analysis of the project. They describe the neural network as a tool that extended the expert's analysis, and they argue that the art historian remains responsible for the key professional and ethical tasks. They do not test the accuracy of the reconstruction.
